about: Why each missed question was missed, in the `syntax` (comment-stripped) condition — the classification that makes the score actionable. Assigned by the suite maintainer after reading every reader answer against the presented file text; the answers themselves are in tools/comprehension/transcripts/ so any judgement here can be re-checked without re-running a model.

classes.ambiguous-syntax: the file does carry the meaning, but the spelling admits another reading and the reader would not commit to one
classes.misleading-keyword: a keyword pulled the reader toward the wrong meaning
classes.not-in-file: the meaning genuinely is not in the file — a finding about what this figure carries, not about the notation
classes.bad-question: the question is outside what the figure claims to show, so no reading of any notation could have answered it
classes.grading-artifact: the reader's answer is correct; the deterministic key failed to accept the wording. A defect in the instrument, counted in the raw score and reported, never dropped
classes.reader-error: the file states it plainly and unambiguously and the reader still missed it

scoring_effect: The raw score counts every one of these as wrong. The adjusted score, printed beside it, credits `grading-artifact` answers and drops `bad-question` items from the denominator. Both numbers are reported; the raw one is the headline.

arp-resolution/q2.note: Only reader 1 missed it, and it answered NOT STATED while quoting the very row that answers it: the `table cache` states 'before the exchange | (no entry for B's IP)'. The other two readers quoted the same row and were accepted.

arp-resolution/q3.note: RFC 826 has the target merge the sender's protocol/hardware pair on receipt. The figure draws only what Host A learns; nothing states what Host B stores. All three readers answered NOT STATED, correctly.

arp-resolution/q4.note: The figure says it twice and neither saying is a statement: an edge labelled '1: heard, ignored' to the rest of the LAN, and the ABSENCE of a reply edge from that node. Reader 3 refused to commit ('does not explicitly say whether they send a reply'); reader 1 committed correctly and was rejected by the key (see per_reader). A missing edge carries no meaning — this project's own founding observation — and 'ignored' is prose inside a label, not a construct.

arp-resolution/q7.note: Both misses are the key's fault. Reader 1: 'The request is meant to obtain B's hardware address'. Reader 2: 'A does not already know B's hardware address'. Both are right; the key lists 'does not know' and 'trying to determine', and neither 'does not already know' nor 'meant to obtain' is a substring of any listed alternative. The same brittleness the --selftest pass caught in q2 and q5, in a question whose canonical answer happened to pass.

arp-resolution/q8.note: Whether the receiver merges the sender's mapping BEFORE it examines the opcode is an ordering inside RFC 826's packet-reception algorithm, not part of the exchange between hosts that this figure depicts. No notation would have carried it. Reported, not dropped.

ethernet-frame/q5.note: The tagged row spells the tag as 'TPID 0x8100 + PCP/DEI/VID', so the three subfield NAMES are present and the three WIDTHS (3/1/12 bits) are not. The question asks for both at once, so a half-carried fact scores zero — a compound-question defect in the instrument as well as a gap in the figure.

ethernet-frame/q8.note: The figure draws the frame from Destination MAC to FCS and states the FCS is CRC-32. What the CRC covers, and that the preamble/SFD sit outside it, is nowhere in the file.

l2-forwarding-logic/q3.note: Readers 2 and 3 answered exactly right — 'whether an entry for the destination MAC is found in the MAC table; if found, forward out the single learned port, if not, flood'. The key demanded a second group containing one of 'unknown'/'not found'/…; 'if not, flood' satisfies neither spelling. Reader 1 happened to phrase it in a way the key accepted.

l2-forwarding-logic/q4.note: All three readers answered 'floods to every port in the VLAN; the ingress port is always excluded' — the class label's own words. The key's second group lists 'except'/'excluding'; the readers wrote 'excluded'. Nothing was misread; the key was.

l2-forwarding-logic/q5.note: The figure's decision path never mentions broadcast or multicast destinations. A real gap: an unknown-unicast frame and a broadcast frame take the same branch in 802.1Q, and this figure shows only the first.

l2-forwarding-logic/q6.note: All three readers gave the filter condition correctly — 'the looked-up egress port is the same as the ingress port'. The key's group lists 'same port'/'same interface'/'the receiving port'; 'same as the ingress port' matches none of them.

l2-forwarding-logic/q7.note: Reader 1 opened 'NOT STATED beyond the general rule:' and then gave the correct answer in full. The scorer treats a leading NOT STATED as a declined question, so a right answer was scored wrong — the instrument's rule, working exactly as specified, on a sentence it was not designed for.

l2-forwarding-logic/q8.note: Whether both ports must be in the forwarding state is spanning-tree port state, outside the learn/lookup/flood/forward/filter path the figure declares. Out of scope for the figure and for the brief the questions were authored to.

rpf-check/q3.note: All three readers answered NOT STATED. The file's only candidate is the edge label `next-hop ge-0/0/1`, which spells 'next-hop' but carries an INTERFACE name, never a neighbour. What the source-ward lookup yields besides an interface is not in the figure.

rpf-check/q6.note: All three readers answered in the figure's own vocabulary: 'it passes when the packet arrived on the "upstream" interface (the one indicated by the RIB lookup); the router accepts and forwards it'. That is the decision node's label read correctly. The key was written from the RFC's vocabulary and demands 'same interface'/'matches'. The reading was right; the two vocabularies never met.

rpf-check/q8.note: All three readers answered NOT STATED. The class label states the failure CONDITION ('arrived on an interface that is not the route back to the source'); the file never states the contrast with ordinary destination-based forwarding, which is what the question asks.

tcp-header/q2.note: The figure declares `field "Sequence Number" 32` and no `description=`. Field semantics — that the value is the first data octet's sequence number, or the ISN when SYN is set — are simply not carried.

tcp-header/q3.note: Same shape: `field "Acknowledgment Number" 32` with no description. That the field is significant only when ACK is set is not in the file, even though the language HAS the carrier for it (`present=`, used on Options in this very figure).

tcp-header/q6.note: `field "Checksum" 16` with no description. Checksum coverage, including the pseudo-header, is nowhere in the file.

tcp-header/q7.note: `field "Urgent Pointer" 16` with no description and no `present="URG"`. The conditionality is expressible in the genre and was not written.

dhcp-lease/q6.note: Whether the client may go on using its address while RENEWING/REBINDING, and what it must do if the lease expires before any DHCPACK arrives, are RFC 2131 §4.4.5 facts the figure never carries. The figure draws the RENEWING and REBINDING state occurrences and the requests they send, and stops there: nothing states that the address stays valid meanwhile, and no expiry path is drawn. All three readers answered NOT STATED, correctly. This is the `bitfield` shape again — the carrier exists (`description=`, used heavily elsewhere in this same figure) and was not written on this path.

fragment-operators/q1.note: That declaration order along a lifeline IS time is the genre's load-bearing implicit semantic, and no line in the file states it. Readers 1 and 3 recovered it from the shape alone ('top-to-bottom position encodes temporal order'); reader 2 refused to commit — 'the file does not explicitly state a general rule for lifeline event ordering outside fragments (though by sequence-diagram convention the higher message would occur before the lower one, that convention itself is nowhere written in this text)'. That refusal is exactly right about the file, and it is the arp-resolution/q4 shape: the figure asserts by structure, not by statement. Not a misreading — no reader read the order backwards or as unordered.

fragment-operators/q3.note: The question presumes a construct this figure does not use: it asks about 'iteration bounds - a lower and an upper number', and the figure's loop carries no numeric bounds at all. Its only statement of repetition is the operand guard prose `operand tries "while no response, and fewer than 3 attempts made"`. Reader 2 answered exactly that ('NOT STATED as explicit lower/upper numbers; the loop's only stated bound is its guard ... which caps it at 3 attempts') and was scored wrong for the leading NOT STATED. Recorded against the instrument, not the language. NOTE THE MIRROR IMAGE, which the raw score does not correct in the other direction: reader 1 was CREDITED on this question by accident — its answer denied an explicit lower bound in the words 'NOT STATED for an explicit separate lower bound', and the literal 'lower bound' satisfied the key's first group. See tools/comprehension/sequence-results.json, which reports the hand-corrected number with q3 dropped for every reader.

fragment-operators/q4.note: Both misses are the key's fault and both are the same three words. Reader 1: 'the messages in its different operands ... have no relative order between each other, but it still requires that the messages within each individual operand keep their own internal order.' Reader 2: 'have no relative order ... within each operand keep the order given inside that operand.' Both are the canonical answer. The key lists `no order` among its alternatives and `no relative order` does not contain it as a substring — the §7 brittleness, surviving into a set authored under the v1.1 discipline. Reader 3 said 'interleave freely' and passed.

measured_against: Question sets as of the v1.0 baseline, after the --selftest key repair; the ARP and RPF figures were re-read from scratch when their keys changed, and every transcript in the tree was taken against the question set it is scored under (checked by --verify).
